items.title: [ScienceDaily] That fresh cleaning smell could be filling your home with nanoparticles
items.content_html: Researchers found that scented cleaners can react with ozone indoors to create billions or trillions of invisible nanoparticles that can penetrate deep into the lungs. The pollution forms within minutes and, in some cases, may produce an inhaled particle dose comparable to or greater than standing near heavy traffic.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists may have misread a 2-billion-year-old clue about Earth
items.content_html: Scientists have found that a famous 2-billion-year-old chemical signature, once thought to record a massive global change in Earth’s carbon cycle, may instead have been produced by local magma, hydrocarbons, and methane-eating microbes. The discovery raises new questions about what was really happening as oxygen transformed the young planet.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Two astronauts who flew farther than anyone before are taking new NASA roles
items.content_html: Artemis II astronauts Victor Glover and Reid Wiseman are transitioning to emeritus status at NASA after their historic journey around the Moon earlier this year. The pair will continue advising and mentoring NASA teams as preparations accelerate for Artemis III and future lunar missions. Their experience with Orion and deep-space operations could prove especially valuable as NASA works toward returning astronauts to the lunar surface.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Zepbound and Mounjaro may turn on the body’s calorie-burning brown fat
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, activated calorie-burning brown fat in obese mice, revealing a potential metabolic effect beyond appetite suppression. If confirmed in humans, the finding could help explain the drug’s powerful benefits and inspire more comprehensive treatments for obesity and diabetes.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] REM sleep paradox: Dreaming may drain the brain’s energy even as fuel supply rises
items.content_html: Scientists discovered a surprising energy paradox in the brain during REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming. Blood supply to the brain begins increasing even before REM starts, but neurons’ immediately available energy, measured as ATP, then drops. The finding suggests that dreaming may require such intense internal processing that neurons consume energy faster than it can be replenished.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
items.content_html: CERN has started replacing some of the Large Hadron Collider’s most important magnets as part of its High-Luminosity upgrade. The new superconducting magnets will produce fields about 40% stronger, allowing particle beams to be squeezed more tightly before they collide. That should create far more collisions for the ATLAS and CMS experiments to analyze, giving physicists a much larger window into the fundamental workings of the universe.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal
items.content_html: Researchers have shown that exotic quantum particles called non-Abelian anyons can perform the full range of operations needed for universal quantum computing. Using 54 qubits on Quantinuum’s H2 processor, they combined braiding and fusion to unlock capabilities that braiding alone could not provide.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] These massive stars could explain Webb’s strangest galaxies
items.content_html: Hubble observations of massive stars in metal-poor dwarf galaxies are revealing clues to why the early universe looks so unusual. Researchers found that stellar winds weaken sharply at extremely low metallicities, potentially allowing massive stars to retain more material and evolve in unexpected ways. The team also found large differences in iron abundance, a key ingredient in stellar winds and supernovae.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] ADHD and autism diagnoses have surged. A massive study may help explain why
items.content_html: A large Danish study found that children diagnosed with ADHD or autism today more closely resemble their peers in the general population than those diagnosed 10 years ago. The shift suggests that rising diagnosis rates may partly reflect broader identification and changing diagnostic patterns, rather than only an increase in the underlying conditions.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A broken rib from the world’s largest T. rex hid a 66-million-year-old secret
items.content_html: A broken rib from Scotty, the largest known T. rex skeleton, contains an extraordinary fossilized network of blood vessels formed while the dinosaur was healing. Scientists used neutron and X-ray imaging to look inside the 66-million-year-old bone without damaging it, revealing details rarely preserved in fossils.

Some tropical trees have evolved a clever way to survive drought by taking in carbon dioxide at night, allowing them to keep their pores closed during the hot daytime and conserve water. By comparing three Clusia species, researchers discovered that this water-saving form of photosynthesis, known as CAM, did not arise through a single evolutionary change. Instead, ancient genome duplications followed by millions of years of genetic reshuffling produced strikingly different strategies, from strong CAM to stress-triggered and hybrid forms.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The LHC just ruled out another hiding place for quantum black holes
items.content_html: Physicists searching through Large Hadron Collider data found no evidence that the machine has been producing microscopic quantum black holes, but the result sharply narrows where such exotic physics could still be hiding. These hypothetical black holes could form if extra spatial dimensions make gravity much stronger at extremely tiny scales, potentially offering clues toward the long-sought theory of quantum gravity.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

🔭 ✏️

Lake Powell has fallen to its lowest level on record after an exceptionally dry and warm winter left the Colorado River Basin with little mountain snow to melt. Lake Mead also reached record lows, raising concerns for a river system that supplies water and power to more than 40 million people. Federal officials have taken emergency steps to stabilize Lake Powell, including sending in water from another reservoir and reducing releases downstream.

items.title: [phys.org] Fire amoeba breaks complex-life heat tolerance record at 63°C
items.content_html:
🎨 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Scientists have identified a new amoeba, Incendiamoeba cascadensis, that can eat, move and reproduce in water as hot as 63°C (145°F) at California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park, setting a record for the highest temperature known to support eukaryotic reproduction. The NASA-supported study, published in Cell on Sept. 22, found that the organism remains active at about 64°C and can recover after five minutes at 70°C, although exposure to 80°C proved fatal [phys.org#1][nasa.gov#1][livescience.com#1][sciencenews.org#1]. The finding challenges the previous 60°C upper limit for eukaryotic growth and reproduction, based on the heat sensitivity of proteins and other complex cellular structures. Researchers said the amoeba withstands the heat by changing shape and forming a protective outer layer; genetic analysis also identified genes associated with repairing heat-damaged proteins [nasa.gov#1][science.org#1][orf.at#1]. The work is relevant to astrobiology because scientists use extreme environments on Earth to assess where complex life might survive on Mars and other worlds [nasa.gov#1][npr.org#1].

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Humpback whale mother may have mourned her dead calf for days
items.content_html: Researchers observed a humpback whale mother staying beside her presumed stillborn calf for hours and possibly days off Australia’s Gold Coast. She maintained eye contact and remained close to the calf in behavior resembling caregiving and nurturing. Scientists say the rare observation may provide new insight into grief, maternal attachment, and emotional complexity in humpback whales.
